# How Companies Are Handing First Drafts to AI, and Where People Step In

> **In short:** OpenAI's recent customer stories show AI handling the first pass on heavy tasks, such as sorting documents, producing property listings and drafting device designs, while people review and decide. The companies report faster work and lower costs, and they also describe where the tools fell short.

Think about the last big pile of work you faced: a stack of emails, a long report, a messy project folder. Someone still has to make sense of it and produce a usable version. Three customer stories that OpenAI published show companies letting AI produce that rough first version, with humans checking it before anything goes out.

## Story one: a property company updates its listings

Heimstaden, a European company that rents out residential buildings, decided to speed up its use of AI. After looking at several platforms, it chose OpenAI's tools, including ChatGPT. The company says it had two goals: help employees do their jobs better and rethink the core processes behind its business.

Heimstaden now uses AI to suggest rental prices, style property photos, write apartment descriptions and check listings against its quality standards. Employees still review and approve each decision. According to OpenAI's announcement, the cost of producing a virtually staged photo in the Netherlands dropped by more than 99 percent, and the company estimates large yearly savings in that market alone. The announcement also says Codex, OpenAI's coding tool (software that helps people write and check computer code), was used to analyze 20,112 property assets, and that half of employees adopted the tools within two to three months.

## Story two: a law firm sorts the paperwork

Ropes & Gray, a North American law firm, is developing its own AI tool with OpenAI. The tool targets transactional diligence, which means the checks a buyer runs on a company's contracts and records before a deal closes. It is a slow job, because a team may need to read thousands of pages.

The tool makes a first pass through those documents, groups related files by theme and drafts summaries and a report in the firm's own format. Lawyers can check the groupings to confirm nothing was missed. The firm compared early outputs with reports that human lawyers had written for finished deals, then adjusted the approach where the drafts fell short. According to the firm, this lets lawyers spend more of their time on judgment and less on reading.

## Story three: an engineering test

OpenAI also described how its models help engineers design physical products. In one test, it used GPT-6, its newest model named in the announcement, along with an AI system it calls Astra, to plan a small device that works with Codex. The AI handled the requirements, the enclosure (the outer case that holds a device's parts), the circuit board and the software. OpenAI says two team members produced the design in under a week as a side project, and a contract manufacturer built a small batch of prototypes in under a month.

The test also showed gaps. The AI did not consistently account for the manufacturer's production limits and assembly details, so people needed several rounds of review. OpenAI says these gaps will shape what future models must do better.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you have a repetitive task, such as summarizing a long email thread or turning notes into a clean report, ask an AI tool for a first draft. Then do the checking yourself.
- **At work or school**: Ask where you lose the most time to sorting or first drafts. Try AI there first, and keep a person reviewing the result.
- **If you're just getting started**: Pick one low-risk task and let ChatGPT produce a first version. Compare it with your own work and note what it got wrong. Spotting those errors is the real skill.
- **If you already use it**: Give ChatGPT a checklist of what a reviewer would look for, then ask it to draft a recurring document against that list. Keep a running note of its common mistakes so your reviews get faster.

## Wrap-up

All three stories follow the same pattern: AI produces the first pass quickly, and people handle review and final decisions. The companies also share where their tools struggled, which makes their experiences useful for anyone planning to use AI. Your next step: choose one repetitive task you face this week, time how long it takes you now, and try an AI first draft on it.
